title: XXL vs. 2X is not a formula: What Old Navy and Lee size charts actually show
summary: XXL and 2X may overlap, diverge, or sit in different parts of a brand's range. Two official charts show why the label is only a starting point—and how to translate it without guessing.
author: Curvy& Editorial

sections.heading: The letters look universal, but the math is not
paragraphs: A recent r/PlusSizeFashion discussion about alternative-brand sizing drew substantial attention to a familiar question: is XXL the same as 2X? Commenters offered confident but conflicting rules about straight and plus sizing. The disagreement is understandable because neither label has one industry-wide measurement definition.

The useful answer is brand-specific. A label can indicate a different grade or fit block, but the letters alone do not prove how a garment was patterned. Official body charts from Old Navy and Lee demonstrate two different relationships between the labels, so a shopper needs to translate measurements before transferring a size.

sections.heading: At Old Navy, XXL and part of 2X meet at size 20
paragraphs: Old Navy's current women's tops chart maps XXL to numerical size 20, with a 48.75-inch chest and 42-inch waist. Its 2X covers sizes 20 and 22. The size-20 line under 2X repeats that 48.75-inch chest and 42-inch waist, while size 22 moves to a 51-inch chest and 44.25-inch waist.

That makes XXL and the lower end of 2X measurement equivalents on this chart, not automatically a full size apart. Yet it still does not guarantee that two actual shirts will have identical shoulder width, armhole shape, length, or finished-garment ease. A semi-fitted cotton shirt and an oversized knit can share a chart row and wear very differently.

sections.heading: At Lee, XXL overlaps 1X more closely than 2X
paragraphs: Lee's product-specific chart for its Ultra Lux straight pant tells a different story. The straight-size XXL, mapped to numerical size 20, lists a 39–40.75-inch waist and 47–48.5-inch hips. Lee's plus 1X, mapped to 18W, lists a 39.5–41-inch waist and 47.5–49-inch hips. Those ranges substantially overlap.

Lee's 2X is 22W, with a 43.5–45-inch waist and 51.5–53-inch hips. On this chart, treating XXL as another spelling of 2X would skip over both the overlapping 1X range and a separate 20W row. Lee also warns that chart measurements vary by style, which is a good reason to save the exact product chart rather than relying on a remembered brand size.

sections.heading: Use proportion to decide between overlapping labels
paragraphs: When two labels cover similar circumferences, compare what the product page says about fit, rise, stretch, and length. For tops, prioritize shoulder movement, bust room, upper-arm comfort, and where the hem lands over the stomach or hip. For bottoms, compare the waist and hip together, then check rise, thigh shape, and waistband construction.

If your waist fits one row and your hips another, a W or X label is not automatically better. Look for the garment whose cut addresses the larger mismatch. A flexible waistband may resolve a small waist difference; it cannot correct a seat, rise, or thigh shape that was never designed for your proportions.
bullets: Translate every label into the brand's numerical size and body measurements.
Check whether the chart is general or product-specific.
Record fabric stretch and the intended fit before comparing two labels.
Use a returnable order when the labels overlap but garment measurements are unavailable.

sections.heading: The practical rule: carry measurements, not a permanent letter
paragraphs: The safest cross-brand workflow is to keep current bust, waist, and hip measurements plus the measurements of one good-fitting garment in each category. Start with the brand's chart, then adjust for the specific cut and material. Do not size up or down solely because a product uses XXL, 1X, or 2X.

Community experience correctly identifies real inconsistency, but no single comment can define every retailer's grading. Old Navy and Lee already use the same labels differently. Individual fit will also change with body proportion and preferred ease, so the most accurate answer to 'XXL or 2X?' is the one built from that product's measurements and construction.

For secondhand listings, ask for the label photo and flat garment measurements. A seller's app-selected size category may translate the tag incorrectly, while the actual chest, waist, or hip width remains useful.

researchNote: This guide responds to a high-engagement August 2026 community discussion and compares current official brand charts. Community explanations are individual interpretations; the chart relationships described here are editorial analysis of the published measurements, not a claim that every garment with the same label is cut identically.
